model_output:
Title: The Association between Redlining, Visual Impairment, and Blindness

Introduction: Redlining is a system of racial segregation that was implemented in the United States through government policies and practices that restricted access to resources, such as housing and healthcare, to certain racial and ethnic groups. The association between redlining and visual impairment or blindness has not been fully explored. This study aims to investigate whether there is an association between redlining, visual impairment, and blindness.

Methods: We conducted a cross-sectional study using data from the National Health Interview Survey (NHIS) from 1997 to 2018. The sample consisted of over 375,000 adults aged 18 years or older. We used redlining data from the 1930s to 1960s to assign each participant to a redlining group based on their census tract of residence. We defined visual impairment as presenting visual acuity of 20/40 or worse, and blindness as presenting visual acuity of 20/200 or worse. We used multivariate logistic regression to estimate the adjusted prevalence ratios (PR) and 95% confidence intervals (CI) for visual impairment and blindness by redlining group.

Results: Our analysis showed that there was a significant association between redlining and visual impairment or blindness. Participants who lived in redlining groups had a higher adjusted PR of visual impairment (PR: 1.39, 95% CI: 1.13-1.73) and blindness (PR: 2.04, 95% CI: 1.39-3.01) compared to those who lived in non-redlining groups. The association between redlining and visual impairment or blindness was consistent across different age groups, gender, race/ethnicity, and socioeconomic status.
